papers.title: EnterpriseVal: Quantifying the Efficacy, Reliability and Value of Generative AI in the Enterprise
papers.authors: Abbas Raza Ali, Muhammad Ajmal Siddiqui, Moona Zahid
papers.abstract: Frontier language models now produce professional deliverables that expert graders judge to match human work on a substantial share of economically valuable tasks, yet most enterprise GenAI initiatives fail to show a measurable business effect and a large fraction of agentic projects are expected to be cancelled. We argue that this is substantially a measurement problem: public benchmarks answer "what can the model do?", whereas a deployment decision requires "is this workflow fit, reliable, safe and worth scaling - here, on our data, under our controls?". We present EnterpriseVal, a use-case-level evaluation system that closes this gap. It comprises (i) a formal specification of the use case and of the frozen socio-technical configuration under test, model, prompts, retrieval, tools, guardrails and human oversight, with an autonomy level and consequence tier that jointly set the required evaluation intensity; (ii) a metric catalogue spanning fidelity, utility, efficiency, reliability, assurance and oversight; (iii) a grading protocol that scales blinded expert judgement with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring through prediction-powered inference; (iv) a two-tier threshold gate, stated as an executable algorithm, that maps metric vectors with confidence bounds to REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE decisions; and (v) a value-and-risk model in which the reviewer catch rate is a measured parameter. We report a pilot across three workflows in a global bank. In credit-memo drafting, human-graded citation precision reached 88% and hallucination rate 1.6% for the best model against gates of 70% and 5%; in procedure transformation, analyst refinement effort fell from an estimated 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document. We separate established results, documented pilot evidence, the proposed system and open hypotheses, and specify the experiments required for full validation
takeaways: EnterpriseVal proposes a use-case-level evaluation system for enterprise generative AI that specifies the workflow, socio-technical setup, metrics, and executable REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE thresholds to judge whether a system is fit, reliable, safe, and worth scaling.

The paper combines blinded expert grading with calibrated LLM-as-judge scoring via prediction-powered inference, and reports a pilot in a global bank where the best model hit 88% citation precision and 1.6% hallucination in credit-memo drafting, while reducing procedure-transformation refinement effort from 27.4 to 2.9 hours per document.

Practically, the framework is meant to address the measurement gap behind weak enterprise GenAI impact by giving organizations a structured way to evaluate deployments on their own data, under their controls, before scaling or rejecting them.
actionItems: Review EnterpriseVal as a use-case-level enterprise GenAI evaluation framework, focusing on the frozen socio-technical configuration, metric catalog, and executable REJECT/CONDITIONAL/SCALE gate design.

Evaluate the framework on an internal workflow by collecting blinded expert grades and calibrated LLM-as-judge scores, then compare metric vectors and confidence bounds against the stated thresholds for decision making.

Ask whether the value-and-risk model, including the reviewer catch-rate parameter and oversight assumptions, is calibrated well enough for your deployment context before using it to scale or reject a system.

papers.title: QuranicMMLU: A Cognitively-Aware Benchmark for Evaluating Generative AI Solutions on Quranic Linguistic Knowledge
papers.authors: Rawan El Ghali, Umm Kulsoom, Anas Madkoor, Dima Faris Alsaudi, Roaa Abdelmagid, Roaa Ibrahim, Raghad Mousa, Hamza Aljaji, Abdullah Khanafer, Abdallah Alkanani, Salah Feras Alali, Rawan Khaled Mohamed, Ehsaneddin Asgari
papers.abstract: We introduce QuranicMMLU, a benchmark for evaluating generative AI on Quranic Arabic across multiple dimensions of linguistic complexity. Existing Quranic benchmarks center on general question answering and semantic retrieval, without probing specific linguistic competencies or stratifying by cognitive demand and verse difficulty. We construct a five-pillar Quranic taxonomy spanning Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, Semantics, and Pragmatics, with 31 leaves covering phenomena from tajwīd and root-and-pattern morphology to occasions of revelation and inter-surah coherence. For each leaf we generate questions stratified by Bloom's cognitive level and verse perplexity, then have LLM as a judge to independently answer and score every item and route the annotations to manual review. The resulting dataset comprises 980 human-reviewed questions, each issued in both open-ended and multiple-choice form. We benchmark 12 systems on these items and find that the Islamic-specialized model leads, yet every system scores higher on multiple-choice accuracy (average 84%) than open-ended answer quality (average 60%): the two rankings agree closely (Kendall's τ=0.73), but multiple-choice scoring hides failures that surface only once answer choices are removed. QuranicMMLU thus offers a rigorous, linguistically grounded framework for evaluating Arabic NLP in the Quranic domain.
takeaways: Introduces QuranicMMLU, a cognitively-aware benchmark for evaluating generative AI on Quranic Arabic linguistic knowledge across five pillars: Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, Semantics, and Pragmatics.

Builds a 980-question, human-reviewed dataset stratified by Bloom's cognitive level and verse perplexity, and benchmarks 12 systems using both open-ended and multiple-choice formats with LLM-assisted annotation and manual review.

Practical implication: multiple-choice scores can overstate performance in the Quranic domain, while open-ended evaluation exposes failures, making QuranicMMLU a more rigorous framework for Arabic NLP assessment.
actionItems: Review the QuranicMMLU benchmark design for the five-pillar taxonomy, Bloom’s-level stratification, and the open-ended vs multiple-choice evaluation split to confirm the assessment scope matches Quranic Arabic linguistic knowledge.

Run a comparative evaluation on the 12 benchmarked systems using both answer formats, with particular attention to whether multiple-choice accuracy overstates performance relative to open-ended answer quality and how rankings change (e.g., Kendall’s τ).

Ask whether your intended Quranic Arabic model deployment can support open-ended evaluation and human-reviewed annotation, since the benchmark suggests multiple-choice alone may mask failures in real use.

papers.title: RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents
papers.authors: Shuai Bai, Jiayong Deng, Yikun Fu, Chang Gao, Xuhao Hu, Mianqiu Huang, Yizhen Jiang, Yuheng Jing, Dehui Kong, Keliang Li, Ning Li, Wanli Li, Dayiheng Liu, Dunjie Lu, Changwei Luo, Que Shen, Zheyuan Wang, Zijian Wang, Jie Wu, Gao Wu, Zhihui Xie, Rui Xie, Haiyang Xu, An Yang, Jiakang Yuan, Yanming Zhang, Jiajun Zhang, Xi Zhang, Zhenru Zhang, Zhuo Zhen, Mingkang Zhu, Bowen Zhou
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have advanced along two separate lines: graphical interaction and software development through code and the command line. Real digital work requires both, interleaved rather than stacked end to end. We study hybrid CUAs that autonomously decide when to explore an interface, implement software, and run and visually verify their artifacts. We introduce RecreationWorld, a five-platform framework built around recreation: given a running reference, an agent must discover its behavior and build a faithful implementation with no prescribed workflow. RecreationWorld provides reproducible environments on Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, and Web, plus a unified harness with native GUI control and coding tools. The running reference serves as an oracle for hidden behavioral tests, providing execution-grounded rewards. We scale trajectory generation with high-quality open-source applications. Models trained on these trajectories improve across five out-of-distribution coding and hybrid computer-use benchmarks and more frequently verify their rendered outputs, providing evidence of transfer beyond recreation. For held-out evaluation, we introduce RecreationBench, comprising 250 diverse tasks across domains and platforms. Reference-grounded programmatic and visual assertions cover action-conditioned outcomes at multiple interaction depths; each is validated on the reference and by human reviewers before the suite is frozen for automatic scoring. GPT-6 Astra leads at 58.1% overall, but passes all programmatic tests on just 2.8% of tasks. Agents reproduce static interface structure more reliably than interactions and computed outputs, while generated applications remain smaller and more monolithic than their references. We release the benchmark, environments, and test suites.
takeaways: Introduces RecreationWorld, a five-platform framework for hybrid computer-use agents that must discover a running reference’s behavior and recreate it without a fixed workflow, spanning GUI interaction, coding, and visual verification.

Uses execution-grounded rewards from hidden behavioral tests plus scaled trajectory generation from open-source applications; training on these trajectories improves performance on five out-of-distribution coding and hybrid benchmarks and increases output verification.

RecreationBench adds 250 validated tasks with programmatic and visual assertions; the results show strong transfer is still incomplete, with GPT-6 Astra at 58.1% overall but only 2.8% on all programmatic tests, implying recreation remains challenging across platforms and interaction depths.
actionItems: Review RecreationWorld and RecreationBench as a candidate evaluation setup for hybrid computer-use agents, focusing on its five-platform coverage, hidden behavioral tests, and validated programmatic/visual assertions.

Run a baseline comparison on the released environments and 250-task RecreationBench to measure transfer across Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, and Web, with separate reporting for programmatic tests, visual verification, and interaction depth.

Assess whether the low full-programmatic-test pass rate and the need for hidden reference-grounded tests create adoption or maintenance risks for using recreation-style benchmarks in your own agent training or evaluation pipeline.

papers.title: CIBuzzBench: A Benchmark for Cross-Lingual Understanding of Chinese Internet Buzzwords
papers.authors: Yifan Wang, Junyu Lu, Qifan Wang, Shun Zhang, Chaozhuo Li, Jiahao Liu, Zhijun Cao, Lingbin Bu, Fanliang Bu
papers.abstract: Chinese social media has generated a vast and continually evolving lexicon of internet buzzwords whose meanings are often non-literal and deeply rooted in local cultural and pragmatic contexts. Existing research has primarily focused on interpreting these buzzwords within Chinese, leaving largely unexplored whether LLMs can transfer such culturally grounded knowledge across languages and accurately convey the intended meanings in English. This cross-lingual capability is also critical for safety, as harmful expressions may obscure their offensive content through culture-specific homophony, euphemism, irony, or coded language. In this paper, we investigate the ability of advanced LLMs to understand Chinese internet buzzwords across languages. To this end, we introduce CIBuzzBench, the first benchmark for cross-lingual Chinese-to-English understanding of Chinese internet buzzwords. CIBuzzBench comprises 3,001 Chinese internet buzzwords annotated with English meaning explanations, English equivalents, category labels, and harmfulness labels. Based on these annotations, we design three evaluation tasks: Meaning Explanation, Cross-lingual Equivalent Matching, and Culturally Grounded Harmfulness Detection. We evaluate representative state-of-the-art proprietary and Chinese LLMs under both English- and Chinese-prompting settings. Our results show that LLMs continue to struggle with the cross-lingual understanding of Chinese internet buzzwords, particularly in fine-grained non-literal interpretation, robust equivalent matching under option perturbations, and calibrated harmfulness detection. These findings highlight the persistent challenges posed by culturally grounded language phenomena for multilingual LLMs and safety-oriented evaluation. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/CIBuzzBench.
takeaways: Introduces CIBuzzBench, the first benchmark for cross-lingual Chinese-to-English understanding of Chinese internet buzzwords, including meaning, equivalents, category, and harmfulness labels.
Builds 3,001 annotated buzzwords and evaluates proprietary and Chinese LLMs on three tasks: Meaning Explanation, Cross-lingual Equivalent Matching, and Culturally Grounded Harmfulness Detection.

Finds current LLMs still struggle with non-literal interpretation, robust equivalent matching, and calibrated harmfulness detection, suggesting challenges for multilingual understanding and safety screening of culture-specific language.
actionItems: Review CIBuzzBench task design and annotations for the three evaluation settings: Meaning Explanation, Cross-lingual Equivalent Matching, and Culturally Grounded Harmfulness Detection.

Run a targeted evaluation of your own multilingual LLM on the 3,001-item benchmark, checking performance under both English- and Chinese-prompting settings and with option perturbations in the equivalent-matching task.

Assess whether your deployment or moderation pipeline can reliably detect culture-specific harmful buzzwords, given the reported gaps in fine-grained non-literal interpretation and calibrated harmfulness detection.

papers.title: Benchmarking the Explanatory Quality of Open-Weight Vision-Language Models in Face Recognition
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have recently been proposed as promising tools for face recognition, as they can produce natural language explanations alongside similarity scores. This capability is considered appealing for face comparisons in forensic contexts, which require decisions to be transparent and auditable. However, existing evaluations of VLMs for that use case focus mostly on recognition accuracy, while the validity of generated explanations remains unquantified. In this work, we introduce a benchmarking framework for VLM-based face recognition that treats explanation quality as a core evaluation axis. We propose two criteria that explanations should satisfy: relevance, i.e., reliance on identity-stable facial features; and faithfulness, i.e., alignment with the visible image content without hallucinated features. We jointly develop a methodology enabling the quantification of relevance and faithfulness of evaluated models, based on constraining model outputs to a structured explanation format that supports automated querying and auditing. Using this framework, we benchmark several families of open-weight VLMs, jointly evaluating face verification accuracy and explanation quality. Our results highlight remaining shortcomings of produced explanations, and emphasize the need for such explanation quality metrics to get a complete picture of model performance. The proposed benchmark and open-source evaluation harness provide a foundation for proper benchmarking and future fine-tuning of explainable face recognition systems.
takeaways: Introduces a benchmarking framework for VLM-based face recognition that evaluates explanation quality as a core axis, not just verification accuracy.

Defines and measures two explanation criteria—relevance to identity-stable facial features and faithfulness to visible image content—using a structured output format for automated querying and auditing.

Benchmarks open-weight VLM families and finds explanation shortcomings, suggesting these metrics are needed for more complete evaluation and future fine-tuning of explainable face recognition systems.
actionItems: Review the proposed benchmark design for VLM-based face recognition, with attention to the two explanation criteria and the structured output format used for automated auditing.
Run a comparative evaluation of open-weight VLM families using both face verification accuracy and the relevance/faithfulness explanation metrics described in the paper.
Assess whether the structured explanation requirement and explanation-quality metrics are practical and trustworthy for forensic face recognition adoption.

papers.title: AutoRecLab: Describe the Experiment, Get the Code!
papers.authors: Moritz Baumgart, Philipp Meister, Justus Krell, Michael Schmidt, Bela Gipp, Joeran Beel
papers.abstract: Empirical evaluation is central to recommender-systems (RecSys) research, but turning experimental designs into executable code remains a manual and error-prone task. We present AutoRecLab, a Python-based autonomous RecSys lab that automates RecSys experiments from natural-language prompts. Given a research idea, AutoRecLab derives explicit experiment requirements, builds and validates a prototype, and iteratively expands it into the requested full experiment. The workflow combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search. In our demonstration, AutoRecLab autonomously implements an explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion study. In a baseline comparison across six algorithms and three datasets, 8 of 9 runs succeed at an average cost of approx- imately $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini.
takeaways: Introduces AutoRecLab, a Python-based autonomous RecSys lab that turns natural-language research ideas into executable recommender-system experiments.

Uses retrieval-augmented documentation lookup, static type verification, and execution-steered tree search to derive requirements, build a prototype, and expand it into a full experiment; demonstrates this on an explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion study.

In a baseline comparison over six algorithms and three datasets, 8 of 9 runs succeeded at about $1 per run with GPT-5.4-mini, suggesting a practical way to automate experimental implementation and reduce manual, error-prone coding.
actionItems: Review AutoRecLab as a workflow for turning natural-language recommender-system ideas into executable experiments, focusing on how it derives requirements, validates prototypes, and expands them into full runs.

Evaluate the reported explicit-to-implicit feedback conversion demo by checking the 8-of-9 run success rate, six algorithms, three datasets, and the stated per-run cost in a comparable RecSys setting.

Question whether the approach’s practical adoption depends on reliable documentation retrieval, static type checks, and execution-steered search for new RecSys experiments beyond the demonstrated study.

papers.title: AutoViewMem: Self-Configuring Orthogonal Views for Conversational Long-Term Memory
papers.authors: Zijie Cao, Xijun Qu, Zhicheng Gu, Xiaoshu Chen, Duanyang Yuan, Yanning Hou, Sihang Zhou, Jianxing Gong, Jian Huang, Yang Mei
papers.abstract: Long-term memory is essential for large language model (LLM) agents to maintain consistency and personalization over extended interactions. Existing memory systems typically rely on fixed granularities or static schemas, but these designs struggle when heterogeneous information, such as preferences, events, constraints, and temporal updates, is embedded in a single mixed representation. The resulting semantic interference makes top-K retrieval sensitive to noise and often leaves relevant evidence poorly ranked. We present AutoViewMem, a data-driven framework that organizes long-term conversational memory into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views before indexing. AutoViewMem discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary view set, and uses these views to guide write-time structured extraction of provenance-grounded memories. This representation-first design moves semantic disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, allowing standard top-K similarity search to retrieve focused evidence without explicit routing or iterative retrieval. We further apply offline consolidation to improve memory compactness and consistency. Experiments on the LoCoMo and PersonaMem benchmarks, under both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B backbones, show that AutoViewMem improves long-horizon question answering and personalization over strong memory baselines while preserving a simple inference pipeline.
takeaways: AutoViewMem is a data-driven long-term memory framework that organizes conversational memories into self-configuring, low-overlap semantic views to reduce semantic interference in mixed memory representations.

It discovers candidate views from interaction traces, selects a compact complementary set, and applies write-time structured extraction plus offline consolidation; experiments on LoCoMo and PersonaMem with Qwen3-8B/14B show improved long-horizon QA and personalization over strong baselines.

The approach shifts disentanglement from retrieval time to write time, enabling standard top-K similarity search to retrieve more focused evidence with a simple inference pipeline, without explicit routing or iterative retrieval.
actionItems: Review the AutoViewMem view-discovery and view-selection components to verify how candidate semantic views are derived from interaction traces and how the compact complementary set is chosen.

Evaluate AutoViewMem against strong memory baselines on LoCoMo and PersonaMem using Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, focusing on long-horizon question answering, personalization, and retrieval focus under standard top-K search.

Question whether the write-time structured extraction and offline consolidation steps preserve provenance grounding and consistency without introducing maintenance or deployment complexity that could affect adoption.

papers.title: Listen Before You Speak: Response Planning from Listener Facial Reactions for Conversational Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Conversational speech depends on dialogue context and the listener's immediately preceding behavior. We propose ReACT-TTS, a two-stage framework that uses a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence to plan the next utterance's emotion and prosody before speech realization. On a strict dyadic MELD protocol, Temporal conditioning yields higher mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance than Text-only across ten seeds, while accuracy remains essentially unchanged. Ablations show that temporal modeling performs best among the visual variants and that an explicit early-to-late difference is unnecessary; correct listener reactions also outperform cyclic mismatches on average. In a contextual-appropriateness study with 20 speech researchers, 76% of judgments prefer Temporal, 9% Text-only, and 15% report no preference. We further connect the predicted response style to a Grad-TTS backbone for end-to-end speech realization. Overall, the results support pre-response listener dynamics as complementary cues for conversational response planning. The source code is available at https://github.com/CYJ1/ReACT-TTS_public.
takeaways: Introduces ReACT-TTS, a two-stage conversational speech framework that plans an utterance’s emotion and prosody from the listener’s one-second pre-response facial reactions before generating speech.

On a strict dyadic MELD protocol, Temporal conditioning outperformed Text-only in mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance across ten seeds; ablations showed temporal modeling was best among visual variants, and a 20-researcher study preferred Temporal in 76% of judgments.

Suggests that pre-response listener dynamics are useful complementary cues for response planning, and the planned response style can be connected to a Grad-TTS backbone for end-to-end speech realization.
actionItems: Review ReACT-TTS as a two-stage response-planning approach that conditions utterance emotion and prosody on a one-second pre-response listener facial sequence before speech generation.

Evaluate whether Temporal conditioning reproduces the reported gains over Text-only on the strict dyadic MELD protocol using mean macro-F1 and VAD concordance across multiple seeds, alongside the visual ablations and mismatch comparison.

Ask whether using pre-response listener facial reactions for response planning is practical to adopt in your setting, given the need for a one-second facial window, strict dyadic dialogue data, and end-to-end integration with a Grad-TTS backbone.
